messages.text: I entered a support ticket for this days ago without response. The unit has already failed

Hi Chris, I'm Hal, HeliumDeploy's technical specialist, and I'm taking this over now.

I'm sorry your ticket sat for days without a reply. Let's work out what's wrong with your Bitfortun BS-2 here so the team gets the full picture.

To start, which of these is closest to what you're seeing?

1. It won't power on at all (no lights, no fan)
2. It powers on but doesn't hash, or the hashrate has dropped to zero
3. It shows an error on the screen or in the web page (for example, chips not detected or an overheating message)
4. Something physical: a burning smell, a popping sound, smoke, or a part that has come loose

If you can, also send a photo of the screen or a screenshot of the miner's web page. If you notice any burning smell or smoke, unplug it now and leave it off.

Equipment and Operating History

Miner: Bitfortun BS-2

Initial setup: September 23, 2026

Failure discovered: November 1, 2026

Firmware: Harlo OS (previously running beta 0.1.50)

Power supply: Mean Well LRS-350-12, 12V / 29A / 348W

Typical operating hashrate: 8.5–8.8 TH/s

Typical power consumption: 150–160W

Operating temperatures: Approximately 40–42°C ASIC and 50–54°C VR

The miner operated reliably for over 31 consecutive days before the failure, with no significant temperature or performance issues.

Failure S.

The B.2 stopped hashing and would not start normally. When powered, the AIO board displayed a blinking red LED, accompanied by an audible clicking sound from within the miner.

Troubleshooting P.

Power Supply Testing

Verified 12V DC output from the Mean Well power supply with no load.

With the BS-2 connected, the power supply output drops to 0V.

Disconnecting the BS-2 restores the power supply output to 12V.

The P. has not yet been independently load-tested.

Controller T.

Removed the Harlo ESP32-S3 controller from the BS-2 AIO board.

The controller boots independently through USB, initializes its display, and eventually makes its web interface accessible.

Successfully performed a complete firmware erase and reflash using the Harlo installer.

The flash completed successfully, including matching MD5 verification hashes.

The controller boots successfully following the reflash.

AIO Board Inspection and Testing

Visually inspected the board and connectors.

No visible burn marks, damaged components, or bent pins.

Measured resistance across the AIO's 12V DC input using a Fluke CNX 3000 multimeter.

Resistance measured approximately 0.2–0.3 Ω.

Meter lead resistance measured approximately 0.1 Ω.

Measurements were identical with the Harlo controller installed and removed.

Current S.

The miner is disconnected from power pending further troubleshooting.

I'm H., HeliumDeploy's technical specialist. Thanks for testing all of this, it saves a lot of back and forth. (Your message was cut off at "the power supply enteri...", so send the rest if there's more.)

Here's how I read your results:

1. **Controller:** It boots on its own, the reflash finished and the MD5 matched, so the ESP32-S3 and Harlo OS look fine. The fault isn't in the firmware.
2. **Power supply:** The output dropping to 0V only when the BS-2 is connected, plus the clicking, fits the LRS-350 shutting itself off because of a short and retrying. Since it gives a clean 12V with no load, the supply is probably doing its job rather than causing the problem.
3. **Board:** This is the deciding test. Take away the 0.1 Ω from your leads and the 12V input reads about 0.1 to 0.2 Ω, the same with or without the controller. That's close to a dead short on the AIO board's input side.

Please keep it unplugged. Powering it into a short again can do more damage.

To finish this off, could you send:

1. A clear photo of the serial number label on the BS-2
2. A short video of the meter across the AIO 12V input showing that 0.2 to 0.3 Ω reading. This avoids powering the unit again.

Once I have those, I'll pass everything to our hardware lead.
The symptoms appear consistent with either the power supply entering protection under load or a possible fault in the AIO power circuitry. We have not yet determined which component is responsible.

That fits what you're seeing, and I'd look at it this way.

Your resistance reading is the strongest evidence, because you took it with the power supply disconnected. The P. can't affect that number, and it settles the question either way.

**One check to tell the two apart:**

1. With the BS-2 unplugged, put the Fluke across the AIO 12V input again.
2. Keep the leads in place and watch the reading for about 10 seconds.

What it means:
- **The reading climbs steadily** (into tens of ohms, then kΩ or OL): the meter is charging the input cap····, so the input isn't shorted. Then the PSU becomes the suspect and a load test of the LRS-350 is the next step.
- **It stays at about 0.2 to 0.3 Ω:** that's a real short on the AIO board's power side. Your PSU is then just shutting itself off under a short, which is what the LRS-350 is built to do, and the clicking is it trying to restart.

If you record that 10-second reading on video, that's the clip I asked for. Please also send the photo of the serial number label, and keep the unit unplugged until then.
Video coming asap, numbers really did not move from 0.3 - 0.5

Thanks, that settles it. A reading that stays at 0.3 to 0.5 Ω and never climbs isn't cap····charging. It's a short on the BS-2's AIO board, on the 12V input side.

What that means:
- **Your Mean Well is very likely fine.** Dropping to 0V and clicking is its protection reacting to the short, which is what it should do.
- **The controller is fine too.** You already checked it on its own with a clean reflash.
- Please keep the BS-2 unplugged from now on.

When the video is ready, send it here with the photo of the serial number label. I'll then pass your full test log and my findings to our hardware lead, so nobody asks you to repeat any of it.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)

I'm H., HeliumDeploy's technical specialist, still on your BS-2.

Thanks for the photo. It shows a white label with a CE mark, a barcode and the code **(number hidden)**. It's on the black housing next to the braided cooling hoses, with your meter leads in the corner.

One thing to confirm: is that label on the miner itself, or on the liquid cooler (radiator or pump)? The "120" makes me wonder if it's the 120 mm radiator's part number rather than the BS-2's serial. If the miner has its own sticker, usually on the case or the AIO board, please send a photo of that one too.

After that, the meter video is the last thing I need before I pass your full test log to our hardware lead.
That image is from the side or the rad, I am not seeing any other labels, do I need to take the system apart?

No, please don't take it apart. Your order number and the radiator label are enough to identify the unit, and there's no reason to open up a liquid-cooled system for a sticker.

The only thing left is the short video of the meter across the AIO 12V input. Once it's here, I'll pass your full test log, the photo and the video to our hardware lead.
